title: Cluster of Laslett | SIJ Pain Provocation | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Test battery and algorithm to identify the sacroiliac joint as the source of low back/buttock pain.
procedure: Four provocation tests, each 3-6 thrusts of gradually increasing pressure: (1) distraction: supine, hands on both ASIS, dorsolateral thrusts, moderate velocity; (2) thigh thrust: supine, symptomatic hip 90° flexion, hand under the sacrum, longitudinal pressure through the femur, higher velocity; (3) compression: side-lying on the asymptomatic side, hips 45° and knees 90°, vertical thrusts on the anterior rim of the ilium, moderate velocity; (4) sacral thrust: prone, palm on S2, vertical thrusts, higher velocity. Algorithm: if the first two tests are both positive, stop; otherwise add compression, then sacral thrust. Originally 6 tests; Laslett reduced to 4 because the other two added no diagnostic value.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain in 2 or more of the 4 tests = SIJ likely the pain source; fewer than 2 positive = SIJ pain unlikely/ruled out.
notes: Specificity rises if the patient's symptoms do not centralize on McKenzie repeated-movement testing. Thrusts are provocation, not manipulation: start gently, a single pressure may suffice. SOURCE ISSUE: the page says Gaenslen's test 'hardly contributes' yet 'was included' in the algorithm; the Gaenslen page states Laslett removed it from the cluster, so 'was included' is most likely a typo for 'was not included'. Alternative battery: Cluster of van der Wurff.

title: Thigh Thrust Test | SIJ Pain Provocation | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Pain provocation test for the sacroiliac joint; part of the Cluster of Laslett and the Cluster of van der Wurff.
procedure: Patient supine, examiner on the asymptomatic side. Flex the symptomatic hip to 90°, place one hand under the sacrum, and apply longitudinal pressure through the femur, 3-6 higher-velocity thrusts with gradually increasing pressure.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain.

accuracy.source: Laslett et al. 2005 (page text mislabels the figures as 'sacroiliac compression test', apparent copy-paste typo)

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value; use within a cluster.

title: Distraction Test | SIJ Pain Provocation | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Pain provocation test for the sacroiliac joint; part of the Cluster of Laslett and the Cluster of van der Wurff.
structure: Sacroiliac joint (anterior ligaments distracted, posterior compressed).
procedure: Patient supine with legs extended, examiner on the symptomatic side. Hands on both ASIS, apply 3-6 moderate-velocity thrusts in a dorsolateral direction with gradually increasing pressure.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain.

accuracy.source: Laslett et al. 2005 (page text mislabels the figures as 'sacroiliac compression test', apparent copy-paste typo)

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value; use within a cluster.

title: Sacroiliac Compression Test | SIJ Pain Provocation | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Pain provocation test for the sacroiliac joint; part of the Cluster of Laslett and the Cluster of van der Wurff.
procedure: Patient lies on the asymptomatic side with hips flexed 45° and knees 90°. The examiner stands behind, places both hands on the anterior rim of the ilium and applies 3-6 vertical, moderate-velocity thrusts with gradually increasing pressure.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain.
notes: Page rates weak clinical value; use within a cluster. SOURCE ISSUE: the API embed for this page is the same YouTube ID as the sacral thrust page (7rxOWC9qoOA); verify which video actually plays.

title: Sacral Thrust Test | Sacroiliac Joint Pain Provocation | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Pain provocation test for the sacroiliac joint; part of the Cluster of Laslett and the Cluster of van der Wurff.
structure: Sacroiliac joint (anterior shear of the sacrum on the ilia).
procedure: Patient prone, examiner beside the bench on the symptomatic side. Place the base of the hand on the S2 spinous process with fingers pointing cranially and apply 3-6 vertical downward high-velocity thrusts with gradually increasing pressure.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar pain.
notes: Page rates weak clinical value; use within a cluster. Shares its YouTube ID with the sacroiliac compression page (see that record).

title: Gaenslen's Test | Sacroiliac Joint Pain Provocation | SIJ Pain Assessment
purpose: Pain provocation test for the sacroiliac joint.
structure: Sacroiliac joint (torsion: one hip in full flexion, the other in extension).
procedure: For the right SIJ: patient supine near the edge of the table, left leg hanging over the edge, right hip and knee flexed to the chest. The examiner presses firmly on the flexed knee toward the chest while applying counter-pressure on the hanging knee toward the floor. Perform on both sides.
positive: Provocation of the patient's familiar symptoms.
notes: Weak clinical value; Laslett removed it from the SIJ provocation cluster.

title: Yeoman Test | Sacroiliitis Examination | SIJ Assessment
purpose: Provocation test proposed for an inflamed sacroiliac joint (sacroiliitis).
structure: Sacroiliac joint; sacroiliitis may be a feature of spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD/Crohn-related arthritis).
procedure: Patient prone near the edge of the bench. Flex the knee to about 90°, hold the distal femur with one hand, fixate the ipsilateral PSIS with the other, and passively extend the hip.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's SIJ or buttock pain.
notes: Diagnosis of sacroiliitis rests on history, laboratory findings and MRI; physical tests are poorly described and unvalidated, so clinical value is questionable.

title: Gillet Test | Marching Test | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Palpation test for sacroiliac joint 'dysfunction' (a blocked/hypomobile SIJ); also called Marching Test or Sacral Fixation Test.
structure: Sacroiliac joint motion between PSIS and S2.
procedure: Examiner behind the standing patient palpates both PSIS (level of the S2 spinous process). For the right SIJ: right thumb on the right PSIS, left thumb on S2. The patient flexes the right hip to 90°.
positive: In a normal SIJ the PSIS drops below S2; in a 'blocked' or hypomobile SIJ the PSIS does not drop or moves only minimally.
notes: Low reliability; value questionable. Physiotutors advise abandoning SIJ dysfunction tests in favour of provocation tests such as the Cluster of Laslett. Related: standing bent-over (Vorlauf) test, Shimpi prone SIJ test, SIJ nutation/counternutation.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Play | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Manual assessment of sacroiliac joint play for suspected SIJ hypomobility.
structure: Sacroiliac joint, described in 4 quadrants (1-2 above S2, 3-4 below).
procedure: Patient prone. For the right SIJ, place the hypothenar of the right hand in quadrants 2 and 4 (on the sacrum) and grasp the ilium with the other hand. Pull the ilium up and medially and assess joint play, avoiding posterior rotation of the ilium.
positive: Not a binary test: judge joint play/end-feel compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a; reliability reference Robinson et al. 2007

notes: Physiotutors advise leaving SIJ dysfunction tests behind due to low reliability and focusing on provocation tests such as the Cluster of Laslett.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Nutation Assessment | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Manual technique to assess sacral nutation for joint play, the little movement available, and pain provocation.
structure: Sacroiliac joint, sacrum divided in 4 quadrants (1-2 above S2, 3-4 below).
procedure: Patient prone with a pillow/bolster under the ASIS of the side examined. Examiner on the asymptomatic side places the hand corresponding to the tested side on the sacrum (right SIJ: right hand in quadrant 2; left: left hand in quadrant 1), other hand on top, and applies a cranioventral force, assessing end-feel or joint play.
positive: Not a binary test: judge end-feel, joint play and pain compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a; reliability reference Robinson et al. 2007

notes: Physiotutors advise leaving SIJ dysfunction tests behind due to low reliability and focusing on provocation tests such as the Cluster of Laslett.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Counternutation Assessment | SIJ Dysfunction Assessment
purpose: Manual technique to assess sacral counternutation for end-feel, joint play or pain provocation compared with the other side.
structure: Sacroiliac joint, sacrum divided in 4 quadrants (1-2 above S2, 3-4 below).
procedure: Patient prone. Examiner on the asymptomatic side places the hand corresponding to the tested side on the iliac spine (right SIJ: right hand) and the other hand on the sacrum below S2. Apply pressure in opposite directions: ilium hand cranioventral (and lateral), sacrum hand ventrocaudal. Assess end-feel or joint play.
positive: Not a binary test: judge end-feel, joint play and pain compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: n/a; reliability reference Robinson et al. 2007

notes: Barely any movement occurs at the SIJ, so isolated movement assessment is hard and reliability is low; Physiotutors advise focusing on provocation tests such as the Cluster of Laslett.

title: Top 5 Gluteus Maximus Exercises
purpose: Exercise selection for gluteus maximus strengthening based on EMG activation (Reiman et al. 2012 review).
structure: Gluteus maximus: powerful hip extensor and lateral rotator, most important for accelerating the body up and forward from about 45-60° hip flexion and in plant-and-cut to the opposite side. Lateral rotation weakness is strongly associated with patellofemoral pain syndrome.
procedure: Top 5 by activation, listed from low to high: 1) retro step-up, 2) wall squat, 3) single-leg squat, 4) single-leg deadlift, 5) step-up; plus Physiotutors' personal favourite, weighted hip thrusts.
notes: EMG activation is only one selection factor; also consider functional needs, joint angle, open vs closed chain, coordination demands, sensorimotor feedback, irritability and patient skill.

title: Top 5 Gluteus Medius Exercises
purpose: Exercise selection for gluteus medius strengthening based on EMG activation (Reiman et al. 2012 review).
structure: Gluteus medius: key stabilizer of femur and pelvis in weight bearing, highest activation in stance phase of gait; anterior, middle and posterior fibres make up 60% of total hip abductor cross-sectional area. Abduction/external rotation weakness is associated with patellofemoral pain via knee valgus, hip adduction and internal rotation.
procedure: Top 5 by activation, listed from low to high: 1) side-lying abduction with/without resistance band, 2) pelvic drops, 3) single-leg deadlift, 4) single-leg squat, 5) side bridge / side plank.
notes: Companion page to the gluteus maximus top 5.

title: Copenhagen Adduction Exercise | Adductor Strain Pre- and Rehab
purpose: Eccentric adductor strengthening for prevention and rehabilitation of hip adductor injuries (frequent in football; low adductor strength raises injury risk).
structure: Hip adductors of both legs (upper leg primarily trained), loaded eccentrically.
procedure: Side-lying on the lower forearm, other arm along the body. A partner holds the upper leg at about hip height, one hand at the ankle and one above the knee. Lift the body with a 3-second concentric adduction while adducting the lower leg until the body is in one line and the feet touch; then lower with a 3-second eccentric phase until the body is halfway down and the lower foot just touches the floor without support. No trunk side-flexion. Suggested start: 2 sets × 6 reps per side, 2-3 times per week, progressing to 3 × 15. No partner: Smith machine with a cushion; progressions: TRX or added weight.
notes: Ishøi et al. 2016 RCT (8 weeks, young sub-elite footballers): eccentric adduction strength +35.7%, eccentric hip abductor strength +20.3%. Harøy et al. suggested adding it to the FIFA 11+ programme to address groin problems.

title: Sacroiliac Joint Pain Exercises | SIJ Pain Treatment | Low Back Pain
purpose: Exercise approach for a painful (sensitized) sacroiliac joint by loading the muscles that provide force closure.
structure: SIJ pain = pain within 2 cm of the PSIS with referral to the Fortin area. Stability via form closure (joint surface configuration, ridged surfaces, dense ligaments) and force closure (rectus femoris, glutes, hamstrings, iliopsoas; latissimus dorsi and erector spinae via the thoracolumbar fascia).
procedure: Examples: clamshell side-plank (progression: quadruped), fire hydrants, iliopsoas march, side planks (progressions: straight legs, upper-leg abduction), single-leg deadlifts, planks, bridging (progression: with leg lifts), abdominal curl, back extensions, supermans, lat pulldown. Let the patient's aggravating activities guide whether to load into extension or flexion.
notes: Causes: sacroiliitis/Bechterew's disease, direct trauma (missing a step), pregnancy/postpartum ligament laxity. Kibsgård et al. 2014: SIJ movement cannot be defined even with laboratory measurement, so hyper/hypomobility 'dysfunction' cannot be palpated; nociception can be tested. Reference: Vleeming & Schuenke 2019.
